utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Monday, January 18, 2010, and I greet our accused, Defence counsel, all members of the OTP in this courtroom, as well as everyone helping us. We are going to hear a witness. He's scheduled for six hours examination-in-chief, which will provide six -- three hours for the other Defences and six hours for the Prosecution, which means that we will be hearing this person for two weeks. Furthermore ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, I would like to say that the Trial Chamber will issue a written decision regarding the request made last week to start the hearing of Mr. Petkovic as February 11. A written decision will be issued and it is a decision that grants the motion made by the Prosecution. I would like to thank Mr. Coric's Defence for having sent us the provisional schedule for March as far as their witnesses are concerned. They will start being called as of March [as interpreted] 22nd, but because of the hearing of Mr. Petkovic starting in -- on February 11, there might be a shift as far as the first witness is concerned, the first witness being planned for March [as interpreted] 22nd. Furthermore, in the written decision the Trial Chamber will invite the Petkovic Defence to call early in February the witness that we could not hear last week. He could come in the time slot made available between February 1st and February 11, and the Trial Chamber is inviting the Petkovic Defence to make all the necessary arrangements to make sure that this witness could be heard before we hear General Petkovic. Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that there has been a mistake in the transcript or in the translation. The 22nd of February is the date we gave, not March. Therefore, we move on to the end of February or the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely you're right. Your provisional schedule -- in your provisional schedule it was February 22nd and there will be an automatic shift. I'll still take the opportunity to tell the Coric Defence that the Trial Chamber will not sit on April 19, 20, 21, and 22nd, so make sure that you don't schedule witnesses for these four days. I believe the Registrar has two IC numbers for us.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Two parties have submitted their lists of documents to be tendered through witness Vinko Maric. The list submitted by 4D shall be given Exhibit Number IC01157 and the list submitted by the OTP shall be given Exhibit Number IC01158. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Mr. Scott, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours. Good morning, Mr. -- good afternoon, Mr. President, each of Your Honours. Thank you for giving me the floor. I will start by -- I won't belabour it, as perhaps unseemly, but I do appreciate and thank the Chamber for the additional time granted in connection with the written order in connection with the Petkovic testimony. The Prosecution is most grateful for that order. Mr. President, Your Honours, I regret, especially in light of that, I regret having to take a bit more of the Chamber's time on a procedural matter, but feel that it is under the circumstances absolutely necessary that I do so. I have prepared in this regard a copy of some materials in the same fashion that we had received them from the Petkovic Defence this weekend. I provided those to the Registry. Perhaps the Chamber has those. And have those been distributed, too? And to the usher, if I can provide one item for the ELMO, please, if you could help us in kind of going through that. Mr. President, each of Your Honours, in connection with the next witness I don't believe there are any protective measures requested, so we could use the name, but in any event it's regarding this next witness who is about to start. As the Chamber well knows, back on the 24th of April, 2008, this Trial Chamber adopted certain guide-lines for the presentation of the Defence evidence. Paragraph 28 of that decision as provided and as is on the ELMO in front of Your Honours provides: "The party presenting the witness must disclose to the other parties and the Chamber a list of all the evidence it intends to present in connection with this witness's testimony two weeks before the said witness appears." Consistent with that in this respect, Your Honours, on about the 4th of January of this year, 2010, the Prosecution received from the Petkovic Defence a spreadsheet or table of exhibits for this next witness with 190 documents on that list. Now, I've provided a copy just now to the Chamber of the spreadsheet of all the exhibits in the form that actually includes a number of things which I'll explain momentarily. That is the list that we received -- or we received the list of the 190 exhibits on the 4th of January, which would have been the approximately two weeks before the beginning of this witness as required by this Chamber's 24 April 2008 decision. However, Your Honour, what happened this past weekend is that in the course of the weekend and I think on Saturday afternoon the Prosecution received a new list, this list totalling 160 exhibits, as you'll see also on the ELMO presentation in front of you. Of that -- of those 160 exhibits, out of the 190 documents that have been identified and listed consistent with the two-week rule on the 4th of January, of those 190 documents only 29 remained the same, only 29 out of 190 remained the same. All the new documents, the balance of 131 documents making up the new total of 160 documents were first provided and first identified to the Prosecution on Saturday afternoon. Your Honour, the Prosecution fully appreciates and would not be on its feet if it was a matter of reducing a larger list to a smaller list because we know that happens, we would not be on our feet if it was a matter of adding two or three or four new exhibits that might have come up in the course of preparing the witness. We understand that happens. It's happened with Prosecution witnesses and if that were the case I would not be on my feet. But what we have in this situation, Your Honours, this is virtually an entirely new list. We get a list of 190 documents two weeks in advance, as required by the Chamber's ruling, and on the Saturday before a Monday start we get for all practical purposes a brand new list. Of 160 documents, only 29 are the same. It's a whole new list. Over the past two weeks the Prosecution office, as we are diligent to try to do, has prepared to meet the evidence of this witness and to assist the Trial Chamber as best we can in cross-examining the witness and providing this Chamber with as much information and assistance as possible. We prepared on the basis of the 190 documents, Mr. Kruger and others read every single document of those 190 documents prepared on that basis. Now on Saturday we are presented with essentially an entirely new list of 160 documents, save 29. It violates the Court's decision of 24 April 2008. It is unfair to the Prosecution, it does not assist the Chamber in getting at the truth, it is an unacceptable practice. I felt compelled to bring it to the Chamber's attention. I know this is scheduled to be a two-week witness and I think the very least, the very least that the Prosecution can ask in this situation is to be ensured -- and maybe that would be the result in any event given this particular schedule, and we might benefit from the particular schedule, but in any event we would ask that the Prosecution cross-examination not start any earlier than next Monday given these circumstances. That might be the case in any event, but the Prosecution only a day -- only less than two business days -- well, not even business days, but less than two calendar days before the beginning of this witness has been hit with essentially an entirely new list of exhibits. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, I listened to what Mr. Scott was saying and I'm a bit flabbergasted, just like he is. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good afternoon to you, and I would like to greet all in this courtroom. Your Honours, in relation to that I have the following to say: The facts that Mr. Scott refer to here are correct indeed. I would like to remind you that it did not happen seldom -- as a matter of fact, it was a rule during the Prosecution case and during the case of the other Defence teams that certain documents be added to the exhibit list or that the parties are notified of new events that a witness would speak of. I wish to remind you that the Prosecution used to notify us during their case of new facts that their witnesses would speak of ten minutes before we would walk into the courtroom. The Defence of General Petkovic never protested because of that in any way, in the belief that we would have enough time during the direct examination to carry out additional investigations and that we would be in a position to cross-examine. I fully agree with Mr. Scott that that could be relatively drastic in the case of today's witness, but I would like to say that the reason may be the fact that this witness was supposed to be heard for six hours, that is to say two or three times longer than other witnesses were heard. So it would be logical that there is a proportional increase in the number of documents that are used. In this entire situation I think that one thing really matters, and that is the following. I'm waiting for my case manager to give me information about this, but I think there are only two documents that are not exhibits involved here. So all these new documents are actually documents that are Prosecution documents to a large extent and also, to a large extent, Petkovic Defence documents. And they have been exhibits for several months or several years. These are documents that were referred to in the opening statement of General Petkovic's Defence, and in this opening statement it was stated quite clearly that the subjects referred to in the opening statement would be discussed by some witnesses and then only certain witnesses would speak about some particular subjects in this regard. Your Honours, I believe that the Defence of General Petkovic did not diminish the possibility for the Prosecution to prepare properly for cross-examination. First of all, these are documents that our colleagues from the OTP are certainly fully aware of; if they're not fully aware of them, they should have become familiar with them by now. Also, since this witness was envisaged for six hours and before the cross-examination there will be the direct examination by the Defence and also

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: cross-examination will start only on Monday. So if our colleagues believe that they nevertheless need additional time to study documents that are already exhibits, documents that they have used so far in supporting their own case, I'm not opposed to that. Can the cross-examination of the OTP start on Monday? That would be fine by me. If we have caused any kind of trouble by this and if we are making them work harder, I do apologise, but I have to present my own point of view. I believe that as far as exhibits are concerned, any party can use them at any point in time during the proceedings. If I've made a mistake, I sincerely do apologise. If you think an additional explanation is required, then I'm here to answer any question you may have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, given the six hours, the three hours, and the questions from the Bench, I'm fairly sure that the Prosecution will not start its cross-examination before next Monday. So Mr. Scott shouldn't run into any problems in this respect. However, personally I would like to state the following. 190 plus 160 is 350 documents, which is a huge number of documents. There are a number of cases here that were judged -- that were actually tried without the same amount of documents, and just for one witness you have 350 documents. That's huge. I note that a great number of these documents have already been seen or commented with other witnesses. So theoretically the Prosecutor should not run into too many problems regarding his questions. He knows most of these documents, but it's still a great number of documents, 350. Mr. -- Ms. Alaburic, I'm a bit surprised. You know, I was in Mr. Scott's shoes at one point in time as well as in your shoes at one point in time, so I know how things work. I'm a bit surprised that you should draft a first list with 190 documents and then suddenly add 160 at the last minute. Normally when you prepare for a witness you should have everything at hand in the first place, but here you added 160 documents after having drafted a first list. To me it's very surprising. Now, since Mr. Scott told us that he would like his cross-examination to start on Monday, I believe that this will happen given the number of hours allotted to the Defences.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not really sure that the computation was correct, the computation by the President. If I understood Mr. Scott right we have 160 documents. So we have 160 documents replacing the 190 documents. Is that it or did I misunderstand you? The second list is replacing the first one and there is -- there are 29 documents from the first list that are in the second list. So you have 160 documents to show to the witness, and all the others you just gave up. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since Judge Trechsel spoke in French, I had to listen to the interpretation. So that is exactly the case. The old list of 100 documents is what we replaced by this new list consisting of 160 documents. That is to say that we are going to show the witness only 160 documents. In view of our experience with witnesses and in view of the fact that these are documents that have been seen many times by now in this courtroom, we believe that we can manage that without any problem whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Alaburic, if I understood you correctly, with the math done by Mr. Trechsel, we have 131 new documents which were not in the first list, the 190 list? Is that it? So there's 131 new documents that were disclosed to the Prosecution on Saturday?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honours. Out of these 131 documents about 100 of them have the status of exhibits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If we add the two lists it would have ended up with 350 documents, but you will only use 160, 131 being new and not on the first list of 190. Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm not going to belabour the matter under the circumstances. We are -- the circumstances may be in some respects a happy one, if I can describe it in that way, in these circumstances because of the particular time-limit. If the witness was -- if the cross was likely to start the next day or two --

utterances.speaker: MS. PINTER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I beg your pardon, Mr. Scott, but there seems to be no interpretation. The gentlemen, the accused do not have any interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you for that, counsel. Can you hear me now? Thank you, counsel, for that assistance. I'll begin again, Your Honours. The circumstances here may be pleasant ones in the sense that given the relief requested and the time schedule of this witness, it may very well be that the cross-examination would not have started until Monday in any event. If that's the case, then it is simply fortuitous that more relief might not have been required. I'm happy for that if that's the case. I do want to correct one shortcomings on my first presentation. I failed to explain to the Chamber - and I do think the Chamber should appreciate this with great respect - concerning the spreadsheet or table that I put before each of Your Honours: The items in yellow or the items that were added; the items marked in red are the items that were removed; and the items in white, if you will, the items that are neither red nor yellow are the only items from the original list that remain the same. All the items marked in yellow are the 131 new items. Once again, Your Honours, as you scan your eyes through that list looking at the colours, you will see that what the Prosecution and in fact now the Chamber has in front of it now is a list substantially different than the one the Prosecution received two weeks ago. I just want to address one other comment by Ms. Alaburic briefly, Your Honours. Every time these issues are raised, the standard response -- and I understand her reasons for making it, but the standard response is well the Prosecution has had all these exhibits for a long time, the Prosecution should know the exhibits. Well, Your Honours, President Antonetti, as you said a few minutes ago, there are tens of thousands of documents in this case, literally tens of thousands. I'm proud of the Prosecution team. I think we know them fairly well. I think I know them fairly well, but I certainly do not have 10.000 or more documents committed to memory. Beyond that, beyond that, the Prosecution is entitled, again, to have a list, not to guess which of the 10.000 might come up, which might be used, but to have the list of -- the Chamber's 24 April 2008 decision requires two weeks in advance. It makes no difference how many times counsel wants to stand up and say well some of them are Prosecution exhibits, some of them are already admitted, some of them are from other co-accused, it doesn't matter. It doesn't matter. We cannot be required to guess from out of a collection of 10.000 or so documents which ones might be used with this witness. I'm grateful for the time already given and I thank the Court for this attention. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think we -- everybody expressed their opinion. Mr. Karnavas, do you have anything to add?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I do, just a minor point on this because I can sympathise with the Prosecution and I can sympathise with the Defence. Be that as it may, when we get a list, we print it out. Somebody has to print it out. Somebody has to number these documents. We read them. And so when we do get a new list, an entirely new list on a Saturday, a staff member has to work on the weekend to re-print a whole set of documents - two, because there's two of us here - and then somebody has to sit -- well, two lawyers have to sit and re-read the documents. And so even though we are familiar with our own documents and the Prosecution documents, there is a great deal of added work. Be that as it may, I understand the Defence also -- somebody comes, they see things from a different point of view, so both sides do have legitimate reasons. My concern is that too much time is being spent on these procedural issues, way too much time, and I would appreciate it if somehow the parties, including ourselves, endeavoured to just limit the amount of procedural matters and we can -- you know, because we're wasting valuable time. So far we've wasted some 20 minutes. So that was my first point. And I don't mean to be lecturing to anybody, but it's just frustrating sitting here. And trust me, I had to work extra hard this weekend to read all these documents, so I'm not very happy either, but I understand putting a Defence case how difficult it is, so I understand what Ms. Alaburic has to go through. Earlier, Your Honours, you indicated in April we would have several days off. I don't know whether the Trial Chamber has already considered or is thinking about it, but the Easter holiday, both for the Catholics and for the Orthodox, is -- I believe it's April the 3rd. I'm only saying that because those of us who are practicing kind of keep track of those things. In the Orthodox religion we usually spend the entire week celebrating that. I was wondering whether at some point the Trial Chamber would be considering whether we would be getting any time because some of us would like to travel to our homes for the holiday season. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We'll look into this. Let's bring the witness into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: In the meantime, having consulted with the President, I just want to make clear that the Chamber accepts the demand of Mr. Scott and grants the Prosecution a delay until Monday to start with cross-examination, unless of course on Thursday they say, "Well, we've seen it and we can start immediately."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you please give me your name, surname, and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Radmilo Jasak, the 13th of October, 1967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And what is your profession and what do you do at the moment?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm an officer of the armed forces of the Republic of Croatia, head of the section for support and finances in the Croatian military academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your rank?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm a brigadier in the Croatian Army. As far as my civilian education, I hold a degree in engineering. I also went to the officer's school of the Croatian Army and I completed a course for strategic management as well as a course in human resources.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like to know whether you've already testified in a trial about anything that happened in the former Yugoslavia or was that the first time that you testified in such a trial?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And can you please read the declaration before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, a few explanations in order to make sure that this hearing goes very smoothly. You are going to answer questions from counsel Alaburic, whom you met this weekend. She will put forward some documents, they are about 160 documents. Once she will have completed her examination, the other counsels representing the interests of the other accused will also have several hours to ask questions, in fact they will have three hours. Once this part of the questions will be finished, from next Monday the Prosecutor, who is on your right-hand side, will ask questions and they will have the same allotted time as counsel Alaburic. The four Judges before you will ask questions based on documents. Every time or when we see some documents we may take the floor, it might not be automatic, but sometimes we may ask questions based on the documents that have been put before us. Since you are a high-ranking officer, you know that you have to be very concise and very precise, so please be sure that you do so when you answer when dealing with the questions from the Defence or from the Prosecution. If you do not understand questions, do not hesitate to ask the question to be rephrased, even if it's a Judge because Judges can also make mistakes, and you find in their questions that there are some inaccuracies, please feel free to say so. You will testify for about two weeks given the time that has been allotted, which means that from today you should not have any further contacts the Defence team of General Petkovic or with the Prosecutor or any other counsel in this courtroom until the end of your testimony which will be at the end of next week. Please also be discreet with any contacts that you may have with any other person outside of this courtroom. Of course you can tell members of your family your impressions, but it should not go beyond the family circle. I should also like to draw your attention on -- and the specific nature of those proceedings. The Defence represented by Counsel Alaburic will ask neutral questions, but the Prosecutor will be entitled to ask very leading questions, asking you, for instance, whether you agree with their case or not; and if you don't agree you say no and you wait for the next question. We have often had incidents between witnesses and the Prosecutors because witnesses did not understand that the Prosecutor could actually question what had been put forward by the witness, but this is actually the role of the Prosecutor. So you will have to listen to the question of the Prosecutor. If you agree with their question, you say yes; and if you don't agree, you say no, and then you wait for the next question to be asked following your answers to the previous questions. Because the Prosecutor plays a role which is different from that of the counsels from the Defence. So this is what I wanted to say, and if at any time you do not feel well, please just raise your hand and say that you are not feeling very well or that you want to have an extra break. We have breaks of 20 minutes every hour and a half in order to have some changes and in order for you to rest as well because you will see that after two weeks you will be absolutely drained, because it is very tiring to answer to questions for over -- for several hours, but this is the way it works here. So make sure that you have good rests and listen carefully to all the questions that will be put to you. So this is what I wanted to say to you. Counsel Alaburic, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I thank you for these instructions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, good day to you.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You have stated part of your CV for the benefit of the Trial Chamber already. Let us run through a couple more details. We have heard about your date of birth. I'll press on now. Please listen to me and confirm the accuracy of what I'm saying. If I get anything wrong, please by all means correct me. As you said, you were born on the 13th of October, 1967, in Imotski, Croatia. You did, however, spend a part of your life in Bosnia-Herzegovina. You hold a degree in engineering. You also completed the staff command school in Zagreb. You started there in September 1993 and remained there until August 1994. You also gave us a list of courses that you completed. Now a number of details concerning your career. Late in 1991 you were involved in organising the Mostar defence. You were a member of the HVO since its establishment in April 1992. Up until the 15th of June, 1992, you worked as the deputy commander of a battalion, and then up until October 1992 you were a battalion commander with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: If I may just correct one thing, it was the 16th of May, not the 15th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I obviously misrecorded this particular detail. 16th of May, deputy battalion commander; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Battalion commander, that was your next duty, you remained in that position until October 1992. After that, you worked with the VOS at the HVO Main Staff. You continued in that position until August 1993. In July and August 1993, however, you worked with Sector North, which is South-East Herzegovina Operation Zone, the Mostar area, and you spent a year in Zagreb pursuing another course, after which you got a job with the Croatian Army in August 1994. You started working in the operative section in the southern front of the Croatian Army. From May 1995 you worked as an assistant head of personnel in the Ston recruitment area. On the 1st of August, 2000, you went back to Zagreb and got a job with the defence ministry as head of the technology section. In October 2004 you took over as department head in the defence inspectorate. On the 1st of March, 2006, you took up the post of head of the IT and logistics department in the military school. On the 1st of May, 2007, you took up your position as the head of a department in the Croatian military college, the department for support and finances. Also, as you said, you hold the rank of brigadier. Mr. Jasak, is all this information correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I listened to the various items on your CV by Counsel Alaburic, and I see that you joined the Croatian Army in August 1994. And so today you are brigadier or colonel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering, I would like to know whether the Croatian Army took into account when working out your seniority the years that you spent within the HVO; or when you joined the Croatian Army in August 1994, did you start at zero years of seniority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, I started from scratch. And my professional -- the record reflects that I started on the 4th of August, 1994, that was the starting date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the Croatian Army did not take into account your military past in the HVO. That is what I wanted to ascertain, and you have confirmed this. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to have more clarity on your actual position. Head of the Department of Administration and Finance, does that mean that you teach administration and finance or that you are the administrator in financial matters and others of the school. Are you mainly teaching or administering?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am department head for support, finances, and budget. As far as support is concerned, you might perhaps better understand the term "logistics." We organise support for all the schools that are part of the Croatian military academy, and that is the section that I'm in charge of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: His Honour asked you whether your job had more to do with teaching or administration. The short answer to that question would be what?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I don't do teaching. My job is about administration.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, which day is considered to mark the beginning of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The 18th of September, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Who recognised that date as the day marking the beginning of war?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The BH authorities, or rather, the authorities of the BH Federation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, in the French translation it says 18th of September, 1992. I would like to know whether there is a mistake there in the French or in English. So which year are we talking about, 1991 or 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The Yugoslav Army arrived in the Mostar area, in Herzegovina, more specifically the Uzice Corps and the Podgorica Corps. Those two corps reinforced by the units of Serb volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: The village of Ravno, does that ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, of course it does. It's a village in east Herzegovina, mostly populated by Croats. In October of that same year, 1991, this village was practically razed to the ground by these units that had previously arrived in the general area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which date is considered to mark the end of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The day the Dayton Agreement was signed, the 23rd of December, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If my math is correct, this would imply that, at least in terms of what the Bosnian authorities actually concluded, the duration of the war was a total of 51 months, four years and three months. Would that make sense to you mathematically?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, arithmetically I think that makes sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a second. We're not going to go into the details, calculations; however, you said that the Yugoslav Army arrived in the Mostar area with the Uzice and Podgorica Corps reinforced by units of Serb volunteers, and you said that this happened in 1991. But if I'm not mistaken in 1991, I would like to know whether Yugoslavia still existed as an international state that was still acknowledged as such.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So this means that as -- Serbs arrived on the territory of the Federative Socialist Republic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, this date that you mentioned under the existing laws of Bosnia and Herzegovina, is that date considered to officially mark the beginning of war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, officially.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: More about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to refer to a Stojic Defence document which has been exhibited, 2D1183. This is precisely how the duration of the war is defined in terms of time-line. The document is not in this binder, Your Honours. I have no particular intentions of using this document. We might bring the document up in e-court, but other than that I just wanted to say that this was actually defined by law in Bosnia and Herzegovina, and that's all I was trying to say. My further questions will not have anything to do with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, as we said, officially the duration of the war was a total of 51 months. Let us try and see how the relations evolved between Muslims and Croats in Bosnia-Herzegovina. In 1991 were the Muslim side and the Croat side working together or were there hostilities between the two?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Back in 1991 both sides were working together. There were no hostilities between them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the situation in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: In 1992, again the two sides were co-operating.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, we know about some clashes between the BH army and the HVO in 1992. Did you know about those too?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I know that there was some minor skirmishes that would normally be dealt with within a 24-hour period.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. And what about 1993, co-operation or hostilities?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: For the most part we can say that there was co-operation up until March 1993; after that, there were hostilities, particularly on the 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the date. We have the wrong date here.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The 30th of June, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you. What about these hostilities that erupted between the HVO and the BH army, did that spread throughout the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When we say the free territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina, what is the area that we have in mind?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The territory under the control of the Croat and Muslim forces, rather, the territory under the control of the HVO or the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the hostilities between the two went on for?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This went on until the Washington Agreement was signed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you remember when that occurred?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: March 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If we were to sum this up, Mr. Jasak, these hostilities between the BH army and the HVO, and if I were to ask you if this went on for most of the war, what would you say?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No, not for most of the war. I would say this covered a minor part of the duration of the war itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Between 20 per cent and 23 per cent of the entire duration?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Roughly about a year I would say.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, what exactly was VOS mean?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This is the military intelligence service of the Main Staff of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What exactly do they do there?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: They gather intelligence on the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If you were expected to explain in the simplest of terms the difference between the SIS on the one hand and the VOS on the other, how would you do that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The VOS gathers intelligence on external enemies. The SIS deals with internal issues across units, internal problems within the army itself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to the Chamber how exactly you went on gathering information or intelligence in the VOS?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: In much the same way as this appears to be done in any army across the world, operative work, reconnaissance, electronically, or by media analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you say "electronically," what exactly do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Gathering any kind of intelligence whatsoever that is on the air, so to speak, anything at all that is available. And then this information or intelligence is used when and if needed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Eavesdropping or intercepting would be a simpler term covering this area of activity; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, you could put it that way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that cover the tapping of land-lines or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No. This would only have been possible by using radio relay communication.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What intelligence service in Herceg-Bosna was in charge of tapping land-lines? Who dealt with that and who had the power to impose any measures?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I don't know who had the power to impose any measures in that area, but in any democratic state this would have been something for a civilian service normally attached to the Ministry of the Interior.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you work as an analyst with the VOS?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, on the topic of wire-tapping is of the utmost interest for me because we saw a document that was the result of wire-tapping, so that's why I'm interested in this. I fully understood that the VOS was dealing with external forces and the SIS was dealing with internal forces. And you stated that there were operational activities, reconnaissance activities, and electronical surveillance of or media analysis. When doing wire-tapping or when looking for electronically monitored communications, you are testifying under oath so you have to say the whole truth, I was wondering whether you wire-tapped international organisations, such as observers of the European Community who were very often staying in hotels or in buildings that could have been wire-tapped very easily or people from UNPROFOR such as the Spanish Battalion because they had communication means, whether they were secured or not secured. I was wondering whether you wire-tapped those people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not eavesdrop on people like that. I never came across that sort of intelligence within the intelligence service. I don't think anything like that ever came our way. The people who were actually manning the equipment that was used for intercepting and eavesdropping were not fluent in any foreign languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I assume that you were listening to conversations of the ABiH as well as part of your eavesdropping activities.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Were you also eavesdropping of the conversation of the VRS or the Republika Srpska, the VRS to be more precise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was wondering whether you would be eavesdropping on the highest representatives of the ABiH, of the VRS, I was wondering whether Mr. Halilovic would be eavesdropped on or Mr. Delic or General Mladic or other high-ranking representative of that sort, were they being eavesdropped on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Everyone and anyone that was on the air, anything that seemed useful. An analysis would then be drawn up and it would be forwarded from the electronics department to the central intelligence department, and then a report was normally drawn up and analysed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that you could eavesdrop on everything. That was possible. I was wondering whether you would be eavesdropping on not only the military staff of the ABiH, but political representatives, so civilians. So there would be political figures. Let's take an example, Dr. Karadzic, for instance, I was wondering whether political figures were also subject of eavesdropping by your services.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're mentioning Mr. Karadzic and other high officials. They obviously communicated over secure communication lines that were not accessible to us. So it is mostly in the field that our service obtained information, not through intercepting calls.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I am sorry, I am just so ignorant as far as technical things are concerned. When you eavesdrop, do you have the possibility of listening to a particular person or do you simply catch a conversation in the air and then you try to detect in some way who it is that is talking?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Well, it wasn't a specific person who was monitored. What was monitored was a conversation that could be intercepted in the air but during combat operations or when combat operations were expected, since that is when eavesdropping was heightened. On the basis of a conversation, one could assume who was taking part in the conversation even if the interlocutors would not introduce themselves. If people introduced themselves, then it was obvious who it was taking part in the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What would you do if a conversation seemed noteworthy and if the persons concerned had not introduced themselves or if you could not even infer who it was, what do you do then?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Then we would say at such and such a time persons A and B conversed and that such and such information was obtained in such and such an area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. What you're telling us now seems considerably different from what we know in the case of the civilian police in terms of tapping telephone conversations of ordinary citizens. So was there this substantive difference?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: You are right in concluding that because these were short-wave military communications, open communications for the most part. Higher commanders were involved in these conversations or on high frequency waves.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, Mr. Jasak, when you analyse all the information that is accessible to you, do you prepare some reports or what is the result of your endeavours?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Do you mean electronic activity or general activity?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: General activity. If there is a difference, could you please explain both to us?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: There is no particular difference. However, reports that were compiled electronically are selected at the very outset. If nothing really matters, then no reports are submitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please speak slower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. Ms. Alaburic is putting a very interesting question. She is asking you how you managed to make summaries of all this. What she had in mind was that there was probably a co-ordination of all information and you actually answered this. Earlier I heard you say we were also involved in operational activities, and when you said that I wondered the following. Did you have agents planted within the BH army or even planted within the VRS, plant that would be giving you first-hand information without the ones that they were working with knowing about your -- the fact that -- so were there any moles? Did you have moles planted within any forces? Did you have such activities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did have such activities, the operative part that has been referred to only really has to do with our persons who had their officials in the field. So information could be obtained in the field and then it was sent to the Main Staff through the operative zones to the VOS, where we worked on analysing this. We included in our reports what we deemed relevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I just react to the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, at the beginning of your answer you were not very clear and that's why it was misinterpreted. So could you please tell us whether you had any moles in the Army of Republika Srpska or in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No, we did not have any moles in the Army of Republika Srpska or the BH army.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... did you have these moles? I mean, it's the basics of your job, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Why didn't you have these moles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We hadn't reached such a stage of development to have something like that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, did you sometimes receive some information from persons who were close to the BH Army or the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Well, such information was received from the ground, but how they reached us I don't know. I don't know how this information was obtained.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You explained to us now how reports were compiled in this centre for electronic operations. Tell us now, were there any reports that brought together all the reports that were received from the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: There were reports of the VOS.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what were the dynamics of these reports?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: These reports were compiled once a day; if necessary, even more often than that if there was more extensive activity going on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us who these reports were sent to?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: As a rule, they were sent to the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, the head of the defence department, the head of the Main Staff, and others who we thought would find them useful every now and then.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In HVO units -- or rather, did the VOS exist in other HVO units?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, was the Main Staff an independent body or was it within a broader body?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The Main Staff was within the defence department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, in this courtroom we saw the plan of the building in Mostar where the Main Staff was. This was the ground floor of that building. Tell me, did I show you that plan that witness Bozo Peric drew for us?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, you did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what is the area roughly covered by the ground floor of that building?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Approximately 150 to 200 square metres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did the Main Staff use any space in the neighbouring building?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: In the neighbouring building there was only one room that was used for the communications centre, and that's where reports were sent to and from; that is to say, where there was the packet communication and where two officials operated in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, Mr. Jasak, if someone from Vitez, for instance, wants to send by packet radio something to Mate Boban, the supreme commander, who would receive that message in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: It would be received by these officials operating the packet radio of the communications centre.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So at the Main Staff in Mostar; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what stamp would be on this message from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The receiving stamp that they used.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, for the intervention, but unless I misunderstood there seems to be an error in either the translation or the answer or perhaps both. I understood the question to be that, on line 21 of page 31, tell us, Mr. Jasak, if someone from Vitez, for instance, wants to send by packet radio something to Mr. Boban, the supreme commander, who would receive that message in Vitez? And the operative term being "who would receive that message in Vitez." And then following on the answer of Ms. Alaburic's next question, she says: "So at the Main Staff in Mostar ..." it's not clear to me how the Main Staff in Mostar would be receiving a message in Vitez. Perhaps that could just be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank my colleague Mr. Scott, he is quite right. We are talking about a message that was being sent from Vitez to Mate Boban. It is not defined where Mate Boban actually is. So Mr. Scott's objection is fully justified and I wish to thank him for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So the message would be received at the Main Staff in Mostar by packet radio, and then my question was: What stamp would be placed on that document that had arrived from Vitez?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The receiving stamp that was used by officials at the communications centre, just like for all other documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, Ms. Alaburic is starting from the assumption that all messages from Vitez to Mr. Boban would be channelled through the Main Staff and you're answering in that respect also. But as far as you know, did Mate Boban personally have a receiver that could enable him to receive directly by packet transmission or by fax any information from the terrain without having to go through the Main Staff? I assume, to supplement my question, that Mr. Mate Boban probably had a fax number. As far as you know, could you tell us whether he could obtain direct information without the Main Staff being made aware of it or the DOD, or did the information absolutely have to go through either the Main Staff or the DOD?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I understood Ms. Alaburic's question to be as follows. If someone wanted to send something from Vitez to Mate Boban via packet radio, what kind of a stamp would be placed there? It would be the stamp of the receiving post. As far as I understood her, she did not ask whether all the post would be brought in. It is certain that that was not the case. However, if someone had sent that, then it would be there. There would be a stamp there. There would be the stamp of that post depending on the code that it had, and in other cases it would be for the Main Staff like everything else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. You're answering my question in part and I thank you for that, but let me give you an example, a very practical example. Let's imagine that Tuta's unit, Mr. Naletilic's unit, is involved. Could he directly send his report to Mate Boban without the Main Staff or the DOD knowing about it? This is very technical, very specific, and I believe it's also essential.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In response to your question, he certainly could have sent it because as a rule direct information did not go to Mate Boban through the Main Staff because he had an office of his own. However, as regards packet radio, that receiving stamp would be placed there if that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that it was possible, but you're adding that it had to go through the Main Staff -- at least that's what I understand from what you answered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. In response to the hypothetical question put by Ms. Alaburic, my answer was as follows. If someone from Vitez was sending something to a specific radio station, then it had to be sent there; however, it could also be sent elsewhere, not necessarily to that specific post.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Technically speaking, let's take unit X, Tuta's unit, for example, because I believe it's important to use Tuta as an example. Tuta is reporting on an operation, but he only wants to report to Mate Boban and no one else. He does not want Mr. Petkovic or Mr. Praljak or Mr. Stojic to be made aware of the report. Can he do it technically?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never heard of any report for Mate Boban that was sent by Mr. Tuta through the Main Staff. He probably had his own line of communication if he wanted to send that report because I never saw any report from Mr. Tuta at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, all of this will be clarified.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, now we're going to move away from packet radio. I thought that all other communications were well-known to all and that we only had to deal with packet radio. So let's talk about Tuta, Boban. Tuta and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Counsel. I apologise for the interruption, but if we're moving off that topic, Your Honour, I do think it's important and I would like to make an observation and request that perhaps counsel can assist us when she says she'll come back to that. I don't think there's been any foundation laid with this witness yet that he's in a position to give this testimony as to how the communications office worked. Today, unless I've missed it, which is very possible, we've only heard the most general description of what his duties were, something in connection with intelligence, something in connection with the Main Staff from October 1992 until August 1993. We really don't know what he was doing. We don't know if he was ever even in the communications room. We don't know if he ever operated a packet machine. We don't know if he's ever seen the packet communication log. So there are a number of questions that have been put to the witness, Your Honour, that I respectfully submit there's no indication yet that this witness has any foundation to answer those questions beyond the mere speculation. I'm reminded -- excuse me, counsel, let me finish my comments. I'm reminded of Judge Trechsel's comments to the witness last week when he purported to know what every possible officer -- artillery officer throughout Herceg-Bosna had ever seen or done. I suggest that that can't possibly be the case, it couldn't possibly be the case for the witness last week, and this witness so far has provided no foundation for suggesting that he could provide that information. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, take what Mr. Scott just said into account, please. I was assuming that he had this knowledge, but obviously Mr. Scott is not convinced of that. So please try and shed some light on this.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's do it like this. We're talking about the communication options generally speaking. Let us talk about the Tuta-Boban avenue of communication to simplify matters. If those two wanted to communicate, were they able to simply meet and talk, and thereby keep each other up-to-date, issue orders, or anything like that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: That certainly would have been an option.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What if Tuta wanted to send a note through to Mr. Boban, could he have done this by courier?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about communication by courier, was that confidential and direct as a rule?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: That would have been the most confidential form of communication as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What if Mr. Tuta wanted to communicate to Mr. Boban about something or other, could they have used the phone?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What if Tuta wanted to dispatch a letter to Mr. Boban, could he have done this by mail?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, why not?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If Tuta wanted to send a letter to Mr. Boban by fax, could he have done that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, why not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it just occurred to me that at least earlier in armies pigeons were also used for communications. Were any pigeons used in the HVO? Near where I live there was the centre of the Swiss Army's pigeons, so I saw them often [realtime transcript recorded in error "off"]. It may sound like a fairytale to the youngsters [realtime transcript recorded in error "young centres"] here, but ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I never heard of anything like that going on. I don't think that was used.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, this is what you've just told us. It was possible to communicate directly, orally, by phone, by courier, by fax. Therefore, could you also tell us what exactly you are basing your answers on? How on earth do you know what forms of communication were possible in Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This would have been feasible for any two persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about the equipment that we referred to, the phones and the faxes, were such things around?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, you're saying that this was possible. But earlier Mr. Scott made a very relevant observation. He wanted to know how you know this. Where did you get your knowledge from? Let me give you an example. Let's imagine President Obama and the connections he may have with a general in Afghanistan. Everyone can say, just like you said, they were in contact by fax or by phone but they might have a private line also. That's what we would -- that's what we want to know. How did you get this information? Are you just thinking out loud, giving us your answer, or do you know for a fact that Mr. Mate Boban and Tuta could be in contact through couriers? We'd like to know whether you saw these couriers, for example, which is why Mr. Scott actually took the floor. He wanted to know on what you base yourself to answer all these questions. Are you answering Ms. Alaburic's question using common sense or do you have very specific information regarding all of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the question by Ms. Alaburic was hypothetical. Would they have been able to do this or that. No reason they would not have. I have no actual knowledge of their communications.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that you have no information regarding this. Let me press this a little further. As far as you know, within the HVO did the supreme commander of the HVO, Mr. Mate Boban, have a satellite phone and can you tell us whether a unit such as Tuta's unit also had a satellite telephone so that those two could contact each other directly, through these satellite links. Do you know whether they had this -- these devices, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't know that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So packet radio, there was a single fact that I wanted to clarify about packet radio communication --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic, I would like to propose a correction in the transcript. On page 37, line 5, I am reported as saying with regard to the pigeons: So I saw them off. That would be like I went with them to the door, I said bye-bye, but I think I said I saw them often, which is not the same. And then I did not speak of the young centres here, but of the young gentlemen here or ladies and gentlemen. Thank you. Excuse me for the interruption.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this was all actually very amusing. I do have to say that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, packet radio communications, let's try to clarify that. Someone from Vitez, for example, I'm sorry for mentioning any names at all because we got tangled up in these facts. All of my questions are purely hypothetical. Let's assume someone from Vitez wants to send a message through to chief commander Boban. This person knows that Boban is in Grude. Can he now use packet radio communications to send this message through to the Grude packet radio setup?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If this person from Vitez believes that Mate Boban is in Mostar or this person simply doesn't know his whereabouts, so he decides to send it through to Mostar, where would this message from Vitez end up?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The communications centre of the Main Staff, the section in which all the messages were being stored.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I'm sorry to have to come back to this, but I don't see that we've made any progression on this. The witness has still given us no foundation as to how he would know that. We still have nothing further other than mere surmise. I can mere -- I can surmise based on general common sense that probably during World War II there were probably telephone communications in most of Germany. I don't know that but it's a pretty good guess, but we still have no information from this witness that he was ever in the communications room, that he ever operated a packet communication, that he's ever seen the log, that he knows the exhaustive means of all HVO Main Staff communications and can sit here and make these answers to Your Honours under oath that these are the exclusive means that it would have gone through the Main Staff. I'm happy to receive whatever evidence the witness wants to give in response to Ms. Alaburic's questions, but there should be some foundation for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm sorry, but this is how I would summarise this remark. Two persons are talking on the phone. Does each of them in that case have a phone? I believed it to be patently obvious that a person needs to be in the possession of a packet communications set in order to send a message and the same applies to a person receiving a message in this way. I think that is perfectly obvious.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, if you believe I'm wrong, if you believe specialised knowledge is required to actually state this, to ascertain this, that one needs appropriate equipment to send a message via packet radio, please explain.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: A packet radio message can only be dispatched from a place where such equipment exists, and the same applies to receiving a message like that. All the HVO units from the brigade level up had packet radio equipment, and that was how they communicated. For example, military intelligence service used the same kind of packet radio equipment in the Main Staff. Packet radio was being used by the VOS too in order to receive and dispatch reports. The same packet radio set was used by everyone in the Main Staff and the defence department. All the intelligence would end up there on a daily basis. We used this equipment to both receive and dispatch reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Court is back in session.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, another couple of questions about packet radio communications. We've spent too much time on this already. We saw when looking at your CV that in the ministry department of Republic of Croatia you were head of the IT and technology department. We also realise that you were head of the IT department in the military school. We also know that you hold a degree in engineering. We might therefore conclude that you know a thing or two about technology; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, could you please speak closer to the mike because interpreters said that they have difficulties hearing you. So please try to speak closer to the mike. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you know a thing or two about technology. Do you also know about the communications equipment?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Have you ever seen a packet radio set in your life?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you know how it works?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you ever use that kind of equipment in the VOS to receive reports from the field?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you in the VOS ever send any reports or anything like that by packet radio?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, at least once a day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you, but the usual kind of request to both of you that please kindly have a certain pause between the questions and the answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for this caution, Your Honour. I do apologise on my own behalf and on behalf of the witness too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, we have a packet radio set that is in the Main Staff. A letter arrives addressed to the president of Herceg-Bosna, Mate Boban. This letter, this document, in writing, this written document, it leaves the packet radio room and who does it go to next?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: It is forwarded to whoever it is addressed to, in this case Mate Boban or his office.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Directly?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Fine. We shall now be moving on to a new topic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if you have any questions remaining about radio communications, please go ahead; if not, we'll just press on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, a couple of words about how the Mostar defence was organised. Can you tell us when the first activities began in terms of organising the Mostar defence?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The whole thing got off the ground sometime late in 1991 by setting up what we used to call village guards.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: City guards in this case; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, you might call them that too.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about those groups, were they unified under a single body, a single authority in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: They were under the Mostar Crisis Staff later on. At first it was only across the local communities. Later on they were all under the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did these defence groups have anything to do with the HVO, which as we know was established in April 1992?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes. The HVO was established based on those very groups at a later stage.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the HVO organised along territorial lines?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes. The principle used was territorial and the same applied to municipal staffs as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What was the task of those municipal staffs of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The task was to defend their respective municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about these HVO municipal staffs, were they intended to be used for the purposes of defending other municipalities too?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No. They were only to be used to defend their own territories, local communes at the outset and then municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about these HVO municipal staffs, were they at one point reorganised as brigades?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Late in 1992 they were reorganised and became municipal brigades to all practical intent. If there was a municipality that could not provide for an entire brigade, then a number of different municipalities would be pulled together as it were.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, again I apologise for the interruption. But I'm going to have to come back to the previous -- to the principle I raised earlier today. I have to tell the Chamber and counsel that I'm going to -- I may do this more regularly than not because I think we've lost a little bit of the thread in the courtroom. Before the witness can give testimony, he has to provide us some foundation for it. Has he ever been to a Crisis Staff? Was he ever in a Crisis Staff in any municipality, let alone speculating as to what all municipal Crisis Staffs did in all municipalities during this entire period of time. That's what he purports to talk about so far. Was he ever in a Crisis Staff? Was he a member of one? Which municipality? What practices did they have or not? What was the policy in that particular municipality? These are gross generalisations, gross speculations by a witness for which there is no foundation yet - maybe there will be - but no foundation yet that he can provide this testimony. I don't think the Chamber is assisted by receiving with due respect to the witness, mere speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, when you ask a question, I wanted to actually to take the floor in the same way as Mr. Scott just did. The witness states that the HVO was organised according to the territorial principle. But I thought you were going to ask the following question: How do you know about this? What allows you to put this to us? But you say nothing and you carry on. So we are wondering whether this is just general information that he has acquired or has he had -- does he have a personal knowledge of the way a Crisis Staff works? Because your questions go to the heart of how the HVO was set up and they also deal with a joint criminal enterprise. So we would need to know how -- what is the foundation which will avoid Mr. Scott to say what he's already said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I believe that the remark by my learned friend Mr. Scott is entirely unfounded. Had he been following closely the part where we talked about the witness's CV, he would have realised that all my questions were stemming from what the witness told us he was doing late in 1991 up until October 1992 when he came to the Main Staff. If you look at the witness's CV, you will see that as of late 1991 he was involved in the Mostar defence. He was a member of the HVO since its establishment in April 1992. We also go on to point out that he was a deputy commander of an HVO battalion in Mostar. We also say that at one point in time he became commander of that same HVO battalion in Mostar. All these facts were clearly stated at the beginning of today's hearing in relation to the witness's CV, which I believe provides more than sufficient foundation for asking these questions.
