If my learned friend still believes that the witness does not have appropriate information and knowledge to answer these questions, then may I please ask him to try and overturn this witness's testimony in cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I listened carefully to the questions and answers -- excuse me, the statements by Ms. Alaburic just now starting at line -- page 45, line 19, and continuing through most of page 46. We heard about battalions, we heard about HVO defence. I still don't see, Your Honour, with the greatest of respect, I see no reference to any experience touching on a Crisis Staff whatsoever. I also -- this witness has also not been tendered as an expert. This is not an expert like some people who have prepared a written report and come to give expert opinion over certain structures or certain processes. With the greatest respect to this gentleman, and I have no reason to -- I won't get -- I won't compete. I won't compete with comments from the other side. With the greatest of respect to this gentleman, who I've never had the pleasure of meeting before, all we know so far is that -- and again with the utmost respect, at the time, at the time, not now, but at the time he was an approximately 26-year-old individual who had something to do, something to do, with intelligence in the HVO during a period between October 1992 and August 1993. After that he went to Zagreb and obtained some additional training, et cetera, et cetera. We have not the slightest foundation in my submission that this witness can tell us anything about Crisis Staffs or how they functioned. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you were 26 years of age -- or perhaps actually 24, so you were even younger. For some when they are 24 they run empires, but you were not part of the Napoleonic empire or army, so one could wonder whether you were in a position from a political point of view to understand how the HVO had been set up. And the counsel asking questions said that you were a battalion commander. It's not because you're a battalion commander that you have an extensive political knowledge. As Judges, we will have to assess your credibility. When you say that the HVO was set up on the territorial principle, could you perhaps explain how you know this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that I could. Mostar comprised a number of local communes. There was a local commune called Zahum, the Balinovac area which is along one of the roads approaching Mostar. The people there organised themselves without anyone's assistance. We tried to get all the people we knew there to set up a night guard system to keep the same thing from happening as had occurred in Ravno previously. At a distance of under 100 metres as the crow flies, from there the Yugoslav army and the volunteers had their positions. We to all practical intents secretly organised ourselves in that particular local commune, and this was the case in other local communes too with our friends elsewhere. These groups later became battalions of the Mostar HVO and they were all united under the municipal staffs along territorial lines, Balinovac, Ilici, Cim, Bijelo Polje, Krusevo, Jasenica and other municipalities too. When the HVO was established, Mostar had a total of nine independent battalions and four independent companies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I see more clearly because you had hands-on experience. You are basically saying that units constituted themselves. You are giving the example of Balinovac because you were there, so you took part in the creation of this unit, and thereafter nine battalions that were autonomous joined the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's right, Your Honour. This worked along territorial lines in these local communes, and then they all came together at one point and made up the Mostar area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. And as for the way the municipal headquarters was working, what sort of knowledge do you have on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can tell you that the municipal staffs provided guide-lines and tried to make them all work together, these battalions that had been set up along territorial lines.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic, but I would like to dig a bit deeper to the foundations. Mr. Jasak, you have several times now said "we did this," "we did that." Who is "we"? And could you perhaps tell the Chamber why you went to Mostar in the first place and what happened there? Who did you join? What was your function, your idea? Because there we are a bit blind at the moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I came to Mostar in 1987. I went to the Mostar engineering school. At the time I was living in Zahum local commune. When the JNA reservists arrived in 1991, I realised that some of my Serb colleagues were among them, specifically from the Nevesinje and Gacko areas. I saw them every now and then back in 1991 wearing a uniform at the university. As to what happened in Ravno municipality, imagine me seeing some of my fellow students wearing the uniform of the army that caused this whole thing to happen. I can tell you what this did to me. It caused in me a desire to join a defence effort to defend from these enemies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, if I understand correctly, in 1987 you were 20 because you were born in 1967. So you studied at the faculty of mechanics and you had fellow students like yourself - and if I understood correctly they were of Serbian origin. And in 1991 when the JNA arrived, you saw your friends, your "Serbian friends" who lived in Gacko and you saw your colleagues or your fellow students joining the volunteers of the JNA units. Is that what you're saying here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You understand me correctly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. I understood that correctly. So those volunteers would join the JNA. Were they coming from Serbia or from the Socialist Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Where were they coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I think the witness was interrupted while answering my question. You have made an interesting account of what happened at the beginning. The last thing you said was that you had a desire to do something for the defence of Mostar against the J -- and now the Serbs I suppose. Now, could you tell us what you did, whom you contacted, what were the next steps?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the time I was living near the house of my late commander, Tihomir Misic. We were introduced and that's how the whole thing started for me. Quite simply, people who lived there talked to one another, talked to those whom they trusted, saying that we should organise ourselves in order to prevent the same kind of thing from happening as had previously happened at Ravno. In 1991 at the foot of Hum hill and near Maslenica cemetery, even though we were unarmed we stood guard to make sure we saw any movements from the surrounding hills in the direction of our village, and if there was danger these guards were meant to avert that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Excuse me, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jasak, towards the end of 199 [as interpreted] was it only the Croats who organised themselves that way or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Only the Croats organised themselves in that way, I mean the Croats were the protagonists of the organisation. A very large number of Muslims from that area were with us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: When you told us that these groups then became the HVO in April 1992, when the HVO was actually established, were Muslim soldiers with you in the HVO at the time?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, now that we're discussing the HVO, were you organised as a professional army? Did you have 24-hour duty or were you organised in some other way?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: We could not be organised as a professional army, round the clock; we worked in shifts. When soldiers were not on the front line, they were nearby at their homes, and their respective company leaders, for instance, knew where each and every soldier was so that everyone could be called up quickly.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In October 1992 while you were still commander of an HVO battalion, was the activity of that battalion of yours organised in shifts or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: While I was commander the battalion operated in shifts.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, do you know what professional manoeuvre military units are?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, I do know.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, what is that?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: These are units that can carry out attacks outside their domicile area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, as a rule are soldiers in such units organised 24 hours a day or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: As a rule, they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Jasak, in view of your experience and knowledge as a military officer, if you wanted to organise your army, particularly for defence purposes, would you have more territorial units or manoeuvre units?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: If we are to defend an area, then it would be territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I thought that Ms. Alaburic would ask the question, but actually she didn't. As we go along with your testimony we realise that you were studying at the faculty of mechanics and then you joined the HVO because a territorial unit was set up. I can fully understand that. But what you didn't say is why at the time you did not go to Croatia to join the Croat army because you only did that in 1994, which means that if you stayed there you will have to ask us why -- you will have to tell us why. Was it to defend the city of Mostar? Was it to defend the Croats? Was it to defend what was motivating Mate Boban's actions or to defend your house? Why did you stay there at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in 1991 I happened to be at the university in Mostar and I saw all of that. I stayed with those people because my parents live in Bosnia-Herzegovina to this day. That is to say, I stayed on to defend Bosnia-Herzegovina, both Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because we were organised jointly. In 1994 I joined the Croatian Army due to certain circumstances because I had not managed to get an apartment in Mostar and I got married then and had a child. Since I was not very well off, if I would sleep at home then my sister wouldn't have a bed to sleep in. So then I moved from Zagreb to Dubrovnik and I was put up at a hotel.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, now I actually understand the big mistake I made at the very outset.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Witness, you told us just now that your home, your parents' home, is in Bosnia-Herzegovina and we said at the beginning that you were born in Imotski in Croatia. Could you explain that to us now?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Well, I was just born in Imotski because the village of Sovici, where my parents live to this day, that is to say the municipality of Grude, is in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Since in the territory of the municipality of Grude there wasn't a maternity hospital, then my mother gave birth in Imotski, in Croatia, and then brought me as a baby to Sovici. From then onwards I lived there up until 1994, I mean in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So you were a citizen of Bosnia-Herzegovina. From the day you were born, you attended primary school there, secondary school?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: That's right. I completed elementary school in Sovici. Then I completed the high school for engineering in Grude and the faculty of engineering at the university of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's just explain these Sovici. Is it the Sovici near Grude or the Sovici near Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Sovici, municipality of Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let us go back to our territorial and manoeuvre units. P907 is the document we should look at now. This is a draft report for 1992 that was prepared by the head of the Main Staff. We have already seen this document a great many times. For starters, let us look at paragraph 3. Mr. Jasak, we see in paragraph 3 that towards the end of 1992 the Main Staff was manned by 30 per cent and that, for example, the command of the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina with headquarters in Mostar was manned 95 per cent. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, does your knowledge and experience allow you to give us your comment on these particular figures?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, because I was in the Mostar at the time. So the Main Staff was manned by 30 per cent because the HVO had a high deficit in terms of commanding personnel. If the -- if the Main Staff were to be fully manned, then lower-ranking units would not be properly manned and defence activities could not be carried out in the right way.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to us why it was necessary for lower-ranking commands to be fully manned?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: It was very important because it was important not to make it possible for the forces of the Army of Republika Srpska to return to Mostar. So that was very important in order to defend and protect the citizens of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jasak, in view of your knowledge and experience, if you want to pursue defence operations is it necessary to be familiar with the situation on the ground and to have the ability to react rapidly to enemy activities?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: In order to successfully carry out defence operations, it is very important to be familiar with the ground, that is to say that the commanders of these units were locals, from that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, such defence tasks, can they be carried out more successfully by locals, the local population [as interpreted], or the General Staff for the entire territory? Let me just correct the transcript. I did not say the local population. I said the local command. That's right.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, it is certain that a local command can do better because they would know everyone very well, each and every individual and what kind of problems they had. So at the time when this report was written there were a lot of discussions going on and people were being talked into doing things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, the transcript does not reflect what you said. What command? What did you say?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I said local command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please repeat it once again. Again it hasn't been recorded properly.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Local command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now let us move on and look at the rest of this report. After the HVO brigades, according to municipalities, the report says that there are 45.000 men in the HVO units, and in the professional units there are 855 members. On the basis of these numbers, what would you infer, Mr. Jasak, was the HVO a defensive army or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The HVO was a defensive army exclusively.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the handwritten sentence. It says that the establishment of brigades led to the disbanding of all the municipal staffs and the units became more mobile. Can you tell us when these municipal staffs were re-established in the sense of becoming brigades?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: That was towards the end of 1992 when municipal staffs were re-formulated, or rather, re-established as local brigades.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At the very end of the report it says that as they were creating their forces in the territory of the HZ HB, the Croatian people defended themselves and the majority of the Muslims. What is your personal view, Mr. Jasak? Did you think that the HVO was defending the Croatian people and the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I thought that the HVO was defending both the Croatian and Muslim people and all other peoples in that area who were not hostile towards it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, let me return on the prominent figures, page 56, line 2, my fellow Judge Trechsel had already dealt with this, but I want to be very clear on this because I believe it's important. We have in evidence a document from General Petkovic, a document he wrote himself, which says that there were 85 officers, 85. Could you please tell us whether these are 85 officers meant to supervise and lead the 45.000 men in the HVO or are these 85 officers among the professional units who are 850 but that there were other officers who were non-professional officers? I would really like to know the following. When General Petkovic said that there were 85 officers, does this encompass all officers within the HVO or only professional officers, career officers? If this is the case, then you would not be considered as a professional officer because you didn't graduate from the military school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that these are 85 officers and 91 NCOs and 685 soldiers. That is a unit of professionals. These 85 officers were not trained officers. They were just in that professional unit. Some were trained officers, but very few of them who had come from the Yugoslav People's Army, then a very small number of them had completed JNA school for reserve officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please tell us whether you are part of these 85 or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I was not among these 85 because I was not a member of professional unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So you're not part of these 85 professional officers. Now, as far as you're concerned, this 45.000-troop-strong HVO army, how many officers were there within this army? And I'm talking about career officers and non-career officers. Could you tell us the breakdown between the two?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During this time there weren't any officers whose permanent job this was, if we can put it that way, who had this by way of employment and who had it registered officially. So all of this was on a voluntary basis. You see this figure of 45.000 people. These were people who had grown from the grass roots, who had proven themselves to be leaders, who had 10 or 50 or 100 men of their own at the outset and who proved to be able and courageous. These people were given the duty of officers, that is to say that they had not been formally trained but learned during the war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're not answering my question, but I will ask you one last question. I'm sure I'll get my answer. Out of those 45.000 troops, the cadres, you know, normally in an army these cadres are either officers or NCOs, could you tell us how many people were there for -- to supervise and lead the basic -- the soldiers, the troops, how many were there, a thousand? 2.000?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The soldiers were under the supervision of their commanders who at one point or other became officers. For example, I was an officer too, but I was not a properly trained officer. I was a commander, hence an officer and a battalion commander, but I had not received any formal military training. But I displayed certain abilities during the war and I was appointed to that position when commander Tihomir Misic was killed. That was my experience. There were very few men who had received proper military training, those who came from the JNA. There weren't many men like that in our units. For the most part the men who proved to be natural leaders were then selected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must infer from this that you cannot answer my question. You can only tell us about your personal experience, but when I'm asking you whether there are 500 or a thousand officers, you can't give us a specific answer. Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I wonder whether everything went well here because when Judge Antonetti asked you about the 45.000 troops, page 58, line 10 -- no, further up I think. Yeah. Page 58, line 2, following. You said: "You see this figure of 45.000 people. These were people who had grown from the grass roots, who had proven themselves to be leaders, who had 10 or 50 or 100 men of their own at the outset ..." and so forth. Now, you start talking about 45.000 and then you say they were leaders and hundred men of their own. There's something that went wrong, I'm sure, perhaps it's a translation. But could you explain what you meant, who you were referring to when you spoke of the people who had grown from the grass roots. Who did you refer to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 45.000 men comprises officers, NCOs, and privates, ordinary soldiers. Officers were commanders, members of commands, brigade commands, battalion commands. These men were appointed also company commanders. Platoon commanders, for example, those were considered to be officers. For example, you have a platoon numbering 35 men. They would have a single officer who was its commander. Nevertheless, this officer normally would not be a person who had received previous, formal military training. They simply proved to be sufficiently skilful and able to control a certain area, to be assigned a line to hold on to and preserve; and that is how certain men became or were turned into officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's clear the reference to the cadres was lost up there. If you look again at the document, the Brigadier Petkovic reports 855 members in professional army units, 85 officers, 91 non-commissioned officers, and 607 privates. If you add that up, you get 846 [sic] in total. So probably it's just a bit superficial calculation or do you have an explanation for this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the original document has this last figure here which is not perfectly legible, really, 670-something, it's difficult to read. I'll give it a try, though. For example, let's assume the last digit is nine, in which case it adds up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Yeah. That would be right, except that it doesn't look like a nine at all but more like the lower part of an eight. But it's probably a negligent error and you would agree that the reading here is the 855 are composed by 670 and some privates, 91 non-commissioned officers, and 85 officers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us move on to the next document, Mr. Jasak, 4D1463. This is a report by the head of the SIS administration, one that he sent to the assistant commander for security. The date is January 1994. We know where you were at that time and I'll be asking you a question about your time with the HVO. A peaceful protest by the soldiers is here announced. They want to know about the salaries, about the salary lists, and about the status of Mostar. In January 1994 the soldiers rallied, requesting an explanation. Did any situation such as this occur during your time with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were a number of situations like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: How did you deal with these? Did you simply issue orders and force people to comply or did you do something else altogether?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: In situations such as these, the only course of action was to mingle with the soldiers and try to talk to them in order to convince them that what they were doing was not right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did military commanders in fact try this, try to talk to these soldiers, try to win them over, the HVO military commanders I mean?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Up until October 1992, during my time there as battalion commander I came across situations such as these myself. The only thing to do was to talk, to persuade, to discuss. Later on I had a number of friends who remained there as commanders and they told me that they were coming across similar problems.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As far as that is concerned, what could you tell us? In the HVO was there a real opportunity to exercise effective command?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No. In the HVO at the time there was no real opportunity to exercise effective command.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, 4D1328.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: I believe that the witness, Mr. Jasak, has mentioned a very important point when he said, and I quote, that: "In the HVO at the time there was no real opportunity to exercise effective command." I believe that the question was also of course rather general in my view, what was asked by Ms. Alaburic, and also the answer. Can we take it that during the whole time and during the -- those years when the witness was there, do you think that your position that in the HVO there was no real opportunity to exercise effective command has been valid for the whole time or are you keep in mind the particular point or a particular timing? If it is so, please tell us. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, with the greatest of respect to Judge Prandler, if he might allow me to just intervene with my apologies -- but before the witness answers the questions, I think we're back to where we were earlier today as to foundation. I completely endorse Judge Prandler's position, in fact I was about to get up and he beat me to it this time. Your Honour, again we go back. This was, we established earlier, something about a 24-, 23-year-old man who had a very junior position at the time, no matter what position he might hold today, and he was never more than a battalion commander at a local level. I mean, I respect him for that. But it's still rather limited in his ability to give such a sweeping generalisation in a case such as this. And again I'm reminded once again of Judge Trechsel's interchange -- exchange with the gentleman last week who pretended to be able to say everything about all HVO artillery officers everywhere. I think it's simply too broad of a statement. And I said I would intervene with my apology to Judge Prandler for doing so, but I think before Judge Prandler's question is answered, with the greatest of respect, the witness should once again give us some foundation for this. Again I've never met the man, but if I was a 24-year-old junior officer at the time, I'm not sure I would be in a position to assure this Chamber that at no time during the conflict, at no place that was claimed to be Herceg-Bosna that the HVO could never exercise effective control. It sounds like a rather sweeping generalisation to me by a rather junior officer.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, Your Honours, I believe my learned friend Mr. Scott has just taken a step that we must not allow to pass unnoticed. If we look at his objections today, we shall soon realise that they have nothing to do with Mr. Scott's entitlements at this stage in the hearing in terms of objecting to my questions. What he's presenting is his own positions and explanations for his positions. I would like to remind the Trial Chamber of the time when I raised the same objection three times in a row to a question by the OTP. I was accused of obstructing the proceedings. I was told that we were facing a professional Trial Chamber, well up to its task. I was told my allegations were entirely unfounded, and I received all sorts of remarks in relation to that. I think at this point in time Mr. Scott should clearly be told what his rights and duties are. If he must object, then by all means he should do so. There is no need to explain his objections since we are facing a professional Trial Chamber well up to its task. Mr. Scott rises to his feet with all these lengthy interventions. If the idea is to obstruct my examination, I can tell him right away that I will not lose the plot, that I know exactly what I want to ask this witness, that he is really well and truly wasting his time, his time, my time, the Trial Chamber's time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I want to say one thing. A battalion has a battalion commander as its commander. It's a larger unit, it's a major -- the rank of major, which is a higher rank, and this is part of a brigade, a larger unit. Therefore, the OTP misstated that the commander was an NCO. That is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Ever so briefly, Your Honour. Foundation -- these -- I'm not interested in obstruction at all, and I think my behaviour over the past three and a half years would confirm that. I am interested in the rules of evidence, however, and I am sure Mr. Karnavas will know, and I won't pretend to know about the practice in the UK, although I might have an educated guess. It is absolutely fundamental for a witness to express -- to give evidence on a topic there has to be some foundation for it. It is a -- I think one of my colleagues across the aisle said at one point it's evidence 101. The witness has to be shown to have personal knowledge and the foundation. Now, to come back to counsel's objection, if she wants a short objection, my objection as I would probably typically make in a United States courtroom is: Objection, lack of foundation. No foundation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Well, I can say to some extent what the practice is in the UK, whether Your Honours wish to observe the practice in the UK, the practice in the United States, some state or other or a hybrid or something else all together, the basic point is that Mr. Scott spent about a page of the transcript really making a submission which belongs much later in the final brief, which is to why he is saying that this witness doesn't have sufficient authority to be believed, his inexperience, and so on. It's a matter of argument. When you look at what Mr. Scott said a few minutes ago, that's what he's doing. A lot of what he's said today ought to wait until cross-examination. If he's saying that there's just not sufficient authority or there's something missing in what the witness can say about his experience, he does get the chance to cross-examine. He's been abusing the objections this morning to argue his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, ever so briefly just to reply, just to reply very quickly. That's getting the cart before the horse. Before a witness can give evidence, the first prerequisite is that there be a foundation for the witness to give that evidence. There would be no reason for any witness in any courtroom, whether it's in the civil law system presumably or anywhere, to give evidence, to spend hours giving evidence only to come back and say well really we spent the last three days hearing this, but you know what when all is said and done there is really no foundation for it. It's the first step in the process. Before we spend hours, that there is foundation. My objection is: Lack of foundation.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, if I may, I would just like to respond. If I may get personal. I have a feeling that Mr. Scott is not sufficiently focused. I have a feeling that he's not closely following this examination. Once this document was displayed to the witness, the witness was asked whether there were any similar situations that he faced during his time there when something needed to be explained to the soldiers. The witness answered that question. He said that a number of situations occurred in which he needed to do some persuading and some talking. Orders themselves would have come to nothing. I don't think we're facing any sort of dilemma there. Could I please ask Mr. Scott to simply go back to that particular portion of the transcript to eliminate any misunderstanding between us. Now, as to whether the witness's answer fits someone's purpose or not, that would call for more extensive analysis if you ask me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... well, you're the one that has the solution. Can you hear me? Colonel, I'm saying that the solution lies in your hands. When Ms. Alaburic is putting a question to you, it's either one way or the other, either you can answer the question or you can't. If you can't, just say: I can't answer. Your question is too general. I cannot answer. But if you have the answer, if you can answer, then say first why you can answer. Lay the foundation, because you were there, because you knew about the document, you knew about the event, you experienced something similar, and that way you can prove and demonstrate that you are able to answer the question. And thanks to this, the Judges will not have to put any questions to you to try and shed light on all of this. So everything is in your hands. According to your answer, the Prosecution will not object because you will either understand that you are well aware of the problem. For example, when we talked about packet communication if you had said at the time: Well, I know packet communication because as battalion commander I used packet communications, then period, everything understood the foundation. Or if you said that as battalion commander I commanded so many men, I know exactly what I'm talking about, then we have the foundation and we know that we are talking to a battalion commander. The difficulty is that we know that you were very young at the time, you were 24. You're older now, unfortunately, but now you're a colonel and one can wonder whether the knowledge that you have now comes from what you acquired after the war or during the war or before the war even. What we want to know is what you knew at the time, what you did. Have you understood this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm aware of all that. And if I may explain further, I said in relation to this document and what's mentioned in it, I myself faced similar problems in my own unit while I was in command. I'm also able to say that the unit numbered over 400 men. It was at the time holding one of the longest lines in Mostar itself at the early stage in the clashes. From the road into Mostar, Ilici, Podhum, stretching all the way as far as the Old Bridge in Mostar. This was the longest line being held throughout the clashes with the VRS in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you are saying in 1992 I'm in charge of 400 men and we are facing the VRS and our front line was going as far as the Old Bridge from the location which I cannot really quote here. I think it's Ilici. So you were heading a 400-men unit and in front of you, you had the Serbs and it was going as far as the Old Bridge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We can see more clearly, but perhaps Ms. Alaburic could have obtained some clarification on this which would have avoided some interventions from here, there, and everywhere. Yes, Mr. Prlic. THE ACCUSED PRLIC: One sentence. I haven't heard answer on question of Judge Prandler.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: That's exactly what I wanted to recall us of. I think first the witness should answer the question of Judge Prandler, and probably my colleague would do good to repeat it; afterwards, I would also like to put a question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, all of you, including Dr. Prlic. The -- what I would like to ask and now I do not have before me the transcript, but my question was that have we been told by the witness before on which basis he based his knowledge that there was no effective control in the HVO at that time. Of course recently Judge Antonetti mentioned the fact which we know that he was commander of a unit of 400 and he had read and was probably drafted packet messages, et cetera. But it is still in my view probably should be a bit enlarged by the fact that on which basis he's telling us that there was no effective control in the HVO during that years when he was commander of a battalion. It is my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may just remind you, you didn't have the transcript in front of you. We were talking about command, not about control.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, would it help because I don't want to be cheeky about it, but we have the transcript. Would it help, Your Honour, if we were simply to read to the witness precisely Your Honour's question. Because the way it was put initially was, with respect, very, very clear. Would that -- I make that offer, Your Honour. Your Honour, I have Your Honour's question in front of me on the screen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stewart. Actually, I do have also before me.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Good, thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: If it will help, then I will repeat and quote what I have said that time. "Can we take it that during the whole time and during those years when the witness was there, does he think that your position is that in the HVO there was no real opportunity to exercise effective command? Has it been, I mean this position, valid for the whole time, or are you keeping it, or do you think that it was in a particular point and a particular timing when there was no control?" It is what I have asked for. Then it is up to the witness to answer to me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, throughout my time with the HVO it was like that. I also said that I experienced things like that in my own battalion. I can specify if you like. Sometime in 1992, in the month of September specifically, soldiers assembled in the cultural institute. They wanted to have their commander over. They wanted to talk to their commander. Why is this missing? Why is that missing? There were problems. I had no choice but to go there and talk to these men. I told them: Listen, now, we've got to defend ourselves. If we allow the enemy to penetrate, the city will have nothing to go on any longer. If I had decided to issue orders instead, these orders would have come to nothing. I would have broken up my own unit, whereas on the 1st of September, 1993, when I was there I talked to my friends who were there and who remained in command of those battalions. They told me that the problems continued, the same kind of problems. That is what my knowledge is based on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Jasak. Frankly, I am not convinced that this particular example which you raised and which you explained to us is a relevant basis for a sweeping comment and a sweeping answer that everything during those years of your fight and work in Herzegovina there was no real control by the HVO, I will say, command. And still I -- frankly, I do not want to make any judgement as far as your position is concerned, but I am not convinced that during those years there was no effective control at all. It would be -- it would have been a disaster for the whole HVO if your statement would be proved as true. But it is up to the issues which have to be further studied and I leave it as it is for the time being. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, Mr. Scott wanted to test your knowledge. So we have a document, 4D1328, dated 20th of December, 1993. The head of the General Staff is Ante Roso. It's no longer General Petkovic and it's no longer General Praljak. It's Mr. Roso. This Colonel Ante Saskor sends a letter of resignation. When a colonel resigns, it means that there are serious matters at stake, so we should try and find out why he has decided to resign. So he's pointing at three directions. He says that he is tired and therefore not able to work anymore, saying: I'm incapable and tired. But what is more striking as far as I'm concerned is paragraph number 2, and he says that and there are local authorities and an informal group of powerful men who in a way stop the brigade and the command from being in charge. And in paragraph 3 he goes further and gives more detail by stating that this group of powerful men are war profiteering and that they are local rivalry. So I would like to go back to the question from my fellow Judge regarding command. What is very important to ascertain is whether you personally were faced with the same obstacles while in command, the same obstacles as those quoted in this document, namely, that local authority or municipal authority constitutes an obstacle for an officer and therefore this very officer is not in a position to discharge himself of his duties. So this document shows that there is a problem. And you were not here last week, but last week another document was showing that several officers stated that there were problems within the HVO. So when I link this document with a document that we were presented last week, I could provisionally conclude that the command activities were not easy, despite what my colleague may think. But this is his opinion and not mine. So given that you were on the ground, I was wondering whether the situation as it is described in this document is similar to what you experienced; or do you have no idea, in which case you can say to Counsel Alaburic that you cannot really -- that you cannot really have a point of view regarding this very document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as to this document, if need be I can specify a number of matters because some of my own experiences were similar. For example, there's a reference here to powerful locals. This doesn't mean that these persons were necessarily members of local authorities. They could have been other people. For example, local pub owners who simply had a lot of money to use. I had similar experiences myself. For example, a problem that I came across back in 1992 in my battalion, there weren't a sufficient number of uniforms to go around and those that we had were threadbare and worn. We had previously mobilised one of these pub owners, so now he wanted to exact revenge. He managed to obtain 15 US uniforms, those were the most -- the trendiest uniforms at the time. He managed to obtain a large amount of beer, put up a barbecue. There was a lot of joy and festivity in the unit. Some people came, they looked like some mods with all sorts of trendy shades and so on and so forth, and this proved to be a problem. It was a problem before I managed to convince those men to take off those uniforms, regardless of the fact that they looked incredibly trendy and all. Another example from a colleague of mine who still works with one of these units. He was proposed, his name was put forward, to become a command -- to become commander of one of these brigades. And then people came over from a different village altogether, saying: We need someone from our own village at the head of our brigade. It didn't matter to them at all that this particular person had been trained by the JNA as a reserve officer, whereas the other candidate had barely received any primarily education. These are two specific examples for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, I'm sorry, witness, the point of departure was it is not possible to exercise effective command in the HVO. Now you have just told us one story, at least the first one, where you told your soldiers to take off uniforms they should not have been wearing and they did take them off you said. You succeeded. So that is -- that was effective command of yours, was it not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that was not command. That meant sitting together for a long time talking and engaging in persuasion. Had I issued an order to that effect, I'm sure that I never would have seen those soldiers again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, Mr. Jasak, what can you do to a soldier who you tell to take that uniform off and he says: No, I won't. And then he just walks away. What can you do?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I can demobilise him, and in that way it will seem that he was awarded and then others would say why wouldn't I do a similar kind of thing so I don't have to go to the front line either?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, if you decide to demobilise someone, is it easy for you to mobilise someone else instead of him?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Hardly, because there was general mobilisation, we had what we had, there were quite a few who had fled from conscription to the seaside and to third countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I would like to thank His Honour Judge Antonetti for having examined on document 4D1320 [as interpreted], so I have no additional questions in regard to that document. P3642 is the document I'd like to look at now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's a small mistake, it's 4D1328.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, 4D1328. It was probably an error. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, the next document is document P3642. Yet again, a report of the head of the Main Staff. Now, for the first half of July 1993 let us see to what extent the situation had changed. Now, if you have no knowledge or no experience to that effect, please tell us clearly that you cannot give us your comments with regard to a particular section. My first question has to do with the fact that there is a reference to clashes between the Muslim forces and the HVO in the Neretva valley. And now he says -- the head of the Main Staff says: "We can state with certainty the members of the HVO did not cause these conflicts." Mr. Jasak, you as a VOS officer, in view of all the information that the VOS had available, can you tell us whether this sentence is correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My next question --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My client seems to be making a suggestion. I haven't exactly understood.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My next question in view of the continuation of the report, it's on page 2 of your document, Mr. Jasak. It says in paragraph 2 -- actually, I'm not going to ask you about Central Bosnia because you already told us that you analysed eastern Herzegovina. The report says: "In Herzegovina the enemy has taken the area along with the road Jablanica-Dreznica and the left bank of the Neretva River from Dreznica to the southern part of Mostar." To the best of your knowledge as a VOS officer specialised in south-east Herzegovina, can you tell us is this statement correct or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This statement is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us roughly what the length of the area mentioned here is?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Well, it's a bit over 30 kilometres, say about 35 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. In this part of the report the one-but-last part in this section, party XY is referred to. Can you tell us who that might be?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: XY party would be the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us your comments with regard to this part of the report. It is stated that at present the equipment for the HVO in -- in respect of the localities that are mentioned in the paragraph above is taking place through the areas controlled by the Army of Republika Srpska. How come if the Army of Republika Srpska is our enemy, Mr. Jasak?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This was during the most difficult moments for the Croatian people. I can tell you specifically about Konjic. The area of Turija, Zabrdje, and Zaslivlje, when they remained fully encircled, then the treatment of the wounded -- or rather, getting the wounded out of there was carried out through the territory of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, did the Croats wish to do so or did they have to with the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This was the only way for these people to stay alive or not to end up in camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In other territories what was the position of the HVO about the Army of Republika Srpska, were they an ally or an enemy?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The Army of Republika Srpska was an enemy.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that it would be the right time to take a break, so perhaps we could now. We'll be dealing with this document some more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, let's have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at the same document now, Mr. Jasak, paragraph number 4, problems. Let us see what the head of the Main Staff of the HVO is saying in mid-1993. What does he think the problems involved are? I cannot deal with all of them, but let's look at 4.2. It says that: "The non-existence of professional and manoeuvre units for assault and special actions is a problem. The existing units have suffered great losses" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We can barely hear Ms. Alaburic due to background noise.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I ask you to switch off one of your microphones? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mid-1993, you're still in the HVO; right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, with regard to the number of professional units and the number of soldiers in these units, was there a significant change in relation to 1992? We've already seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Nothing special.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What do you mean, nothing special had changed?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Nothing special had changed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Or in other words it was roughly the same number of soldiers there?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Paragraph 4.4, the following problem is referred to: "Disrupted system of command and mutual co-ordination ..." And now there is an explanation in brackets. "Co-operation among zones, units within zones, and zones with the Main Staff ..." Mr. Jasak, do you have any knowledge about the claim made in this paragraph?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: The previous documents showed that nothing special had changed in this regard.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us look at 4.5 now. It says: "Serious shortcomings in the command system and especially unprofessionalism on the level of squad-company-battalion, and let us be honest, on the level of the zone-HVO staff." Tell us, is this statement true that there weren't enough trained and professional soldiers -- officers and NCOs?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: It is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, when we say "officer," it doesn't automatically mean that that is someone who is trained as a soldier or as an officer?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: That's right. When we say "officer," we are not saying that the person necessarily has a higher education and that he had completed a particular kind of school.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: On the basis of what did such a person become an officer and get some kind of rank?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: On the basis of his hitherto-demonstrated abilities in terms of organising the HVO, in terms of what he had proven up until then during the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at 4.6 now. The following is a problem as well. I quote: "The expectation that the HVO army will resolve everything by itself militarily and on the front. That is to be expected and that is the task of the army. We still do not have such an army - with a modern organisation that is technically well equipped with a resolved command system. "In order to create such an army, the authorities must do far more at all levels and this must be their primary task." In view of your experience in the HVO, could you agree with this assessment?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I could and I do agree with what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us try to analyse this problem of the command system in a bit more detail. Tell us, on the basis of VOS experience, the units on the ground, did they report regularly, comprehensively, and properly about everything that happened on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: As for the VOS, the reports that we received that is, we had our own people at the level of the operative zones, that is to say at higher levels, who regularly submitted reports to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: At this point in time, I'm more interested in the content of these reports. Can one speak about reports from the field in terms of brigade commanders, operation zones, et cetera? Did these reports contain complete and accurate information about developments on the ground?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: There were report -- there were problems in reporting from the field.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you know of the higher commands giving some kind of instructions as to what reports should be like, what their structure should be?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Well, some instructions were being provided, but there was the problem of the level of the persons who were supposed to write these reports, for them to be trained enough or educated enough to carry this out in practice.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now the last part of this report says, I quote: "Practice tells us that the army is becoming privatised - every municipality, every town and village have their 'own' army. It is not possible to move a 'municipal' army from the area of the municipality, and by that very fact, the deployment of stronger forces, adequate to the task is not possible." On the basis of your very own experience in 1992 and your knowledge from 1993, while you were in the HVO, are these assessments correct?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: These assessments are correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there any municipalities that from the point of view of finance and logistics supported their municipal brigades respectively?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: There were such municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us now, as an analyst and an intelligence person, the fact that you are providing financial resources and logistics for a brigade, does that affect the influence of municipal leaders over that brigade? What would you conclude?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Of course such a possibility is open. I mentioned that in the case of the appointment of the brigade commander. It says he's not from our village, no matter how professional he may be. Or in some municipalities where a brigade consisted of personnel from different municipalities, that is to say if there couldn't be enough people from one municipality then it was very important who would command the brigade, a person from which municipality and the like.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 3D793, could we have a look at that now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, we all looked at this document P3642 dated January 22nd, 1993. You might not know that on July 22, 1993, General Praljak replaced General Petkovic at the head of the Main Staff. So this maybe is his -- it's like a testament, you know, he is getting stuck in a situation and reporting on the situation to the head of the DOD. When looking at the document you note that the situation is quite difficult. There are a number of problems. For example, at the last paragraph, according to General Petkovic there are privatised armies and each municipality every time a village have their "own army." So it's a very dire statement made by General Petkovic here. He seems to be saying that he cannot exercise his command. And at item 4.4 he actually says that the system of command is disrupted off and on. This is what he describes. Now, you were an analyst within the VOS. Could you tell us whether on the ground you felt this situation, you experienced this situation, and could you tell us how you actually experienced the change of command, when command shifted from General Petkovic to general command [as interpreted] or was this beyond your -- way beyond your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, paragraph 4.4, disruption in the system of command. I was aware of the fact that there was a situation of that kind in the Ljubusko Brigade and the Operative Zone of South-East Herzegovina. As for the arrival of General Praljak -- or rather, the fact that he became head of the Main Staff, I did not feel that anything special had changed, except for the fact that General Praljak was a bit more energetic than General Petkovic in his issuing of commands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The third party XY is being mentioned in this document. In this document we see that there is procurement of ammunition, of equipment, and limited quantities. General Petkovic says that this third party is a political puzzle. Now, you were in the field. Did you know that sometimes there were agreements with the Serb side even though it was an open conflict going on, but that sometimes obviously there were agreements on a number of things, for example, the passage of troops, the procurement of weapons, and so on? Did you know about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as for activities with the Army of Republika Srpska, I only have information about Konjic, Turija, Zaslivlje and Zabrdje, that's the only problem I'm aware of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You did not know that there were some agreements with the VRS, you were not aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know about any particular agreements with the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I have my answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, do you know anything about the agreements reached under the auspices of UNPROFOR and the international community in which the Serb side was involved too, the VRS, Mr. Martic?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I heard about those under the auspices of the international community, but my understanding of His Honour's question was that the question was about Mr. Petkovic's agreement with all of the three warring factions agreeing.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 3D793 is our next document. We're still dealing with command and effective control. The date here is the 7th of November, 1993. The document is a list of conclusions from a meeting of military commanders. Mr. Jasak, if you look at the signatures there, what can you tell us? Are these HVO brigade commanders and operation zone commanders?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: These are operation zone commanders, brigade commanders, and other high-ranking officers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the transcript, earlier we saw a document, the resignation of Colonel Ante Saskor, and then we -- here we see the name of Ante Saskor, he was attending this meeting. It's on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can provide a perfectly simple explanation. Mr. Saskor's resignation on the 22nd of December, 1993, and this meeting actually took place a month and a half before. Therefore, he still occupied the same capacity at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, are these the highest-ranking officers of the HVO, if we leave aside those at the Main Staff who either couldn't attend the meeting or were not on the list?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: These are the highest-ranking officers from these two recruitment areas: Tomislavgrad and Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Say a conclusion is reached at a meeting like this, would this conclusion be based on anything or not? Would you say that these people were familiar with the situation on the ground or not?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I am looking at the list of names and these are the best-qualified people in terms of judging the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Could you please look at item 6, paragraph 6, of these conclusions. It says that a single line of command should be established. You say you recognise the names and actually know some of the people mentioned there. Would you have any reason to believe that these people didn't in fact know what they were talking about?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No, no reason at all to do anything less than trust these people.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document, P3314 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'd like to ask you a few follow-up questions regarding this document. We all know this document. It was mentioned at several occasions. Did you know that high-ranking officers had met on November 7th, 1993, and that they had made seven recommendations for Mr. Boban for parliament, for the government, and for the Main Staff? Were you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at this and I see them providing certain recommendations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to know what you knew at the time, on the ground, as the British say, the Americans, at the time, on the ground, did you know that officers, high-ranking officers had met and had drafted this document addressed to the political authorities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that there was a meeting and I know that a document was written up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it would be nice if you would precisely answer the question. You say: I know that. The question was: Did you at the time know before or latest on 7 November 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before and on the day itself, no, I did not know. But I found out within that very week that they had met. I didn't know about the substance of the document itself, but I knew that they were facing significant problems and that they addressed the problems at this meeting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And, if I may, second question. The point number 6, six words is very laconic: "Establish one and only command line." Can you explain -- do you understand, and if so, can you explain what is meant with this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I couldn't know at the time what precisely they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Now you stress, very correctly, at the time. I'm asking you now: In hindsight, from today looking back or from an earlier point in time looking back, can you explain -- can you explain what this means, what the contents of this is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't say specifically in relation to this sentence of what it meant. It clearly shows, however, that the line of command was disrupted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, I would not agree to that because it does not say that the command line must be re-established. It says that there should be a single one and there are different explanations as to what the more than single could be, but I will not insist as you have quite correctly said you don't know. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, I am talking --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Would the witness refrain -- would the accused refrain from -- no, I'm not giving you the floor. I'm just telling you that you should not make gestures and start speaking. You could influence the witness and that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, please look at me -- THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Microphone not activated] [Interpretation] I should have been asked about what was done at the meeting. It's my meeting, my position, my conclusion. I spent 55 days sitting at that meeting. I was never asked what it meant specifically, what it meant about the line of command being disrupted --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: And then the interpreters couldn't understand the rest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Colonel, General Praljak's intervention has just demolished the question I wanted to put to you, but I'll put it to you anyway. When learning of this document I'm trying to place it back in the right time-line. After four years of trial, a Judge as humble as may be, must be able to place a document within the right time-line and the political and military time-line of the time. Here we have a document dated November 7th, 1993. I know also that General Praljak left his position as commander of the HVO at the time. I'm trying to see whether there's a link between these two events. This is a document where General Praljak is leaving his office. When reading the document, we see a certain number of high-ranking officers are challenging the command or actually challenging the fact that there is more than one line of command and so forth and so on. And the highest political authority, i.e., Mr. Boban, finding out that there is a problem is going to solve the problem by replacing his Chief of Staff and appointing Mr. Ante Roso at that post. Then Mr. Praljak is jumping up and saying: I organised the meeting. It's his point of view. It would have been better if he had just remained silent and waited for my question and waited for your answer. Now, you were working within VOS, and your assignment was to analyse the situation relevantly if possible. Do you think that there could be a connection between this meeting of high-ranking officers with these nine recommendations and the departure of General Praljak from his post?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I can't allow myself to speculate on that, the VOS analysed the enemy. At the time this document was produced, I had already been in Zagreb for two months being trained --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there is a misinterpretation here. The witness said that he could not speculate. Therefore, this is a misinterpretation. The witness said that he cannot allow myself to speculate on that and the VOS analysed the enemy, but the witness might as well repeat the answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... clear. You are saying that in November you had been in Zagreb for two months already. Therefore, you cannot answer my question. I thank you for your answer, at least it's very specific. But I believe Judge Mindua has a question also.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I'm interested in the form of this document. You're not one of the signatories, but I would like to know the following. We have a list of commanders and officers on the second page. Is this just a list of the people who attended the meeting or is it a list of all people who signed the letter, the signatories to the letter?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please be asked to repeat. The interpreter didn't understand the answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, my apologies. Again the answer was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, could you please repeat. The interpreter says he didn't understand the answer. Can you please repeat.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I do not know which of the people whose names are here actually signed this. I don't know if all these people were there. I did say, however, that I knew about the meeting when I was back home from training. Over the weekend I would meet people and I knew at the time that they had written some sort of a letter about these problems. I did not, however, know what exactly the letter said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. I'm struck by this document. I know that you're not a legal expert, you're an engineer, but in a lot of countries military law when you have multiple claims there is a sanction about that and especially in the armed forces. And in this document we seem to have some proof that there was some proof or evidence of rebellion. So this is to be -- this seems to be a general claim coming from several people. Is that how you also read this document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I would agree with you that this was an act of rebellion if we were talking about a well-organised system. Since the system was what it was at the time across Herceg-Bosna and in the HVO, I would not qualify this as an act of rebellion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this was an army that was working on the basis of civilian organisations. They could fight if they wanted to, they would be answerable to their superiors if they wanted to; is that what you're trying to say here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as far as the army was concerned most of the names here were not qualified to become military officers, which is normally the case in other countries where the rule that prevails is: Carry out the order and then complain. That is why to a certain degree I can understand this. These people have something that was transferred from the previous system.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now that you've mentioned the previous system, is that self-management, is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, roughly speaking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You were 26 at the time. Did you notice among your own soldiers some elements of this self-managing mentality, such as that they felt they had the right to be part of any decision-making progress or being involved in everything that was going on?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I did mention something along these lines earlier on. They invited me to reach an agreement when they assembled in practical terms. Why should we be on our way there, why not someone else? So the only solution was to meet the soldiers and explain to them why something was the case; otherwise, there would have been total chaos.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: These soldiers you were talking to like that, when they were not on duty what did they spend their time doing?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: When they weren't on duty, they would go back to their jobs for which they were qualified. Some of them were farmers, some of them pursued other lines of business or activity.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Plumbers, mechanics, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, all sorts of trades, depending on their professional qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Next document is P3314. I want to know about this particular circumstance. There were soldiers and civilians leaving Kostajnica. The report claims that the army refused to follow anyone's orders. Likewise, commanders from Kostajnica had no control whatsoever over the soldiers. Mr. Jasak, while you were being proofed did you get a chance to read this report carefully?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you personally experience anything similar or did you perhaps hear about anything similar?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I heard about situations like these happening, when positions were taken by the enemy, for example, when the units were withdrawing. Normally there would be no figure of authority in situations such as these who would be able to exert any influence over them.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Do you specifically remember about when certain positions fell and situations in which it was impossible to control the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I see a reference here to Kostajnica that is in the Neretva River valley.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What about when Jajce fell, what was the situation like?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Very much like this. When Jajce fell, this is something that my friends and colleagues told me, when they arrived in Tomislavgrad, they blamed everyone else. Whenever some positions were taken by the enemy, the men were frustrated. Their houses had burned down, they had left their homes, they had left their lives behind. These were, after all, not professional soldiers. They were just ordinary men.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: 3D1099 is our next document. The Stjepan Radic Brigade head addresses his own superior, the commander of the Mostar recruitment area. We're talking about December 1993. You're no longer with the HVO, but let's take a look at what's going on here. The brigade chief sent the following report to his superior.
