"In relation to your order dated the 5th of December, 1993, I herewith report: Where do you get the nerve and courage to order anything at all? If I wanted to correspond with you, I should come down to a level which is intellectually and morally adequate to you. You moron." Mr. Jasak, given your knowledge and experience, could you please comment on this from the perspective of communication within the chain of command. Here we see an example of how a commander addressed his superior, the commander of a recruitment area.

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This is a clear disruption in the command and control system. Having seen a letter like this, there can be no further co-operation between these two. If you look at something like this, were something like this to happen in a normal, organised system following the order issued by a commander, it would be severely punished.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, do you have any personal knowledge about animosities between military commanders within the chain of command or perhaps just in terms of co-ordinating their activities?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I have no personal knowledge about that, but it was more like everyone did as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. 4D1298. This is an SIS report from September 1993. It's about the citizens and soldiers from Livno municipality. It says, among other things, that they're not really that interested in Bosnia-Herzegovina [as interpreted], whereas their main concern is their municipality. Their horizon only stretches as far as the borders of their own municipality. They have no will to fight. They are frustrated that they have to send 120 of their soldiers to Uskoplje [realtime transcript read in error "Skoplje"]. They do not agree with the orders of the Main Staff to transfer weapons to active front lines. They also go on to state that their own fire-power in terms of artillery is reduced by this by about 40 per cent, that they also raise their voices against mobilisation and the fact that their machinery is being taken away in order to build roads. They say unless the vehicles -- unless the machines are returned, they will not be able to maintain 200 kilometres of mountain roads leading to the front line. Finally, they believe that all artillery pieces and weapons are the property of Livno. 200 kilometres of mountain roads, I'll just repeat this part. All the machinery and equipment belongs to Livno and cannot be transferred to other fronts even by order of the GS, Main Staff. Page 93, line 3, the place name is not Skopje, it's Uskoplje.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Ms. Alaburic, I wonder whether an error or slip of the tongue has not occurred. I read you here reading on the report on page 92, line 24/25: They are not really interested in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If I look at the paper I read HB in both language. Would that not rather be Herceg-Bosna than Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're quite right, Your Honour, I did say "Herceg-Bosna."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jasak, I'm going to ask you the following now. As an intelligence person you received this kind of report and you're supposed to infer some conclusions. What would you think about the possibilities of the Main Staff to command the brigade in Livno?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: There would be a problem here, obviously, because the Main Staff should issue orders through the operative zone, or rather, the military district. What comes to the fore here is something that has already been said. Municipal armies, or, rather, municipal brigades, it is obvious that these people are not prepared to help their neighbours put out a fire, as it were. They waited for their own house to be on fire, and it's only then that they would start putting out the fire.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Mr. Jasak, could you please tell us the following now. In 1992 you were in units for the most part, and in mid-1993 in the Main Staff. As for this period do you have any knowledge whatsoever about military operations or military actions that were planned or carried out under the command of the Main Staff of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: As regards military operations and commands of the Main Staff, I only know of an order to defend ourselves as best we could using the resources we had. As for attacks, I'm only aware of one organised operation in November 1992. Bura was its code-name.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, let us look at 2D12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we have looked at three documents, and those documents have to do with the Stjepan Radic Brigade, the Kresimir IV Brigade, and the Cikota Brigade, and this happened from September to December. Those three documents show that there were problems within those brigades. It seems that we could also do the same thing with other brigades, as we saw with a document regarding the meeting on the 7th of November. It seems that the situation is rather dire within the command structure. There are insults, there are cases of insubordination, there seems to be other cases where political authorities are challenged or involved, and I'm sure that if we looked at other documents we could have countless examples. But of course you were no longer there because you were in Zagreb. What I wanted it know is when you were in charge of this battalion, did you feel that there was a problem within the command structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, when I was battalion commander, discussions with company commanders as to what we should do and how we should do it was the kind of thing that I considered to be only natural. I couldn't know how to command otherwise. Command was: Let's discuss it. Let's just go out and do something. Nothing else could have worked otherwise. For you to tell someone that he had to do something, I think that that would have caused a revolt and we would not have attained our objective. Trying to persuade people who had spent a long time at the front line and who were getting a bit of a rest to go back to the front line, is something that you could have done only in that way, by discussing it and by trying to reach a common view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Jasak, on the basis of what we've said so far it would seem that the HVO was a sort of wartime army that came into being during the war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Well, as far as the HVO is concerned, it did come into being during the war. It was established out of nothing, so it can be considered to be a wartime army.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: During your training in these military structures and during contacts with the representatives of foreign armies, NATO, et cetera, did you familiarise yourself with the amount of time needed to establish an army in view of command and control and so on? How long does it take to establish an army that would be called an organised army from that point of view?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I did come across that, and in a system that was set up to a maximum four years was a minimum; that is to say, to have a system of command and control that was established as is the case in modern democracies.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That is one of the topics that is very important for the establishment of the HVO, and that's why I put this question to you. So we said Operation Bura, 2D1935 is the document that I'd like you to look at now. It's -- it's an order for defence. Operation Bura, or Tempest, and the date is -- 2D1295 is actually the number. So I'd like to have that corrected. That's right. I would like to hear your comments about paragraph 5 of this order establishing the tasks of the Mostar Brigade. Can you tell us which army this Mostar Brigade belonged to?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: This brigade of Mostar belonged to the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, was Operation Tempest carried out in co-operation with the members of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Tell us, Mr. Jasak, was the HVO an exclusively Croat armed force consisting of ethnic Croats only?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: No. The HVO consisted -- or rather, the units of the HVO consisted of Muslims -- or rather, Croats and Muslims and all others who were prepared to oppose the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Were there any Muslims in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: Yes, there were and some held very high commanding positions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Jasak, did anyone prevent a Muslim who wished to become a member of the HVO from doing so?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: I have no such knowledge and I don't think that anything like that was ever done. Everyone who wanted to fight the Army of Republika Srpska was welcome.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, were they discriminated against on the basis of any criterion? For example, were they paid less? Did they spend more time at the front or did they have less rest or was there anything else?

utterances.speaker: RADMILO JASAK
utterances.text: There was absolutely no discrimination --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I was hoping not to get back on my feet again, I was trying very hard not to, but we've gone backwards now to calling -- asking broad, speculative questions of this witness with no foundation. He's now speaking for all of the HVO during this entire period. I don't think he can say to the question at line 8 on page 97: To the best of your knowledge, Mr. Jasak, did anyone prevent a Muslim who wished to become a member of the HVO from doing so? There cannot possibly be any basis for the witness to answer other than he can say, to my knowledge I -- to my personal knowledge I don't know. He can't go further than that. The same as to the one just now. "Tell us, HVO soldiers of Muslim ethnicity, were they discriminated on the basis of any criterion," for all of the HVO between 1991 and 1994? I don't think the witness can give that answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, we will have to conclude because we are running out of time. When you touched upon this question you had asked the witness if there were Muslims under his command and he said yes. And it is from this basis that you should have touched upon other issues which would have avoided Mr. Scott from intervening because he may have had some knowledge when you are in charge of 400 men, and we don't actually know how many of those were Muslim. And as Mr. Karnavas says, you could have proceeded step by step.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was going step by step, but no matter what I do there is no way of avoiding interventions by my colleague Mr. Scott, because he's really not paying attention to what is going on. I established that he was a commander of a military unit, I established that there were Muslims in that military unit, and I put the question in such a way that he should tell us about his knowledge. I'm not asking him about an objective fact that prevailed in a broader area. I'm asking him whether he had any personal knowledge about anyone being discriminated against. He can have personal knowledge as a commander, as an inhabitant of Mostar, as a person who is studying in Zagreb and who is in contact with other persons. He can have a million sources of information. I think that my question was perfectly proper and that the colleague [as interpreted] by Mr. Scott was totally unfounded, and had he been following things closely he would not have objected. Your Honour, is it time for us to call it a day or shall I put some more questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I think we are going to end here today because it's almost 7.00. You have used an hour and 31 minutes. You have four hours and 29 minutes left. Witness, you will come back tomorrow for a hearing that will start at 1415. However, be warned, on Wednesday we will have our hearing at 9.00 in the morning and on Thursday it will be again at 1415. So I hope that you have taken note of this. Tomorrow it's at 1415, Wednesday it's at 9.00, and Thursday it's at 1415. And until then, of course, please have no contact with anyone apart from your family. Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, just something for the transcript. My mistake. I did not announce it on time. The document that we used, P3314 is a protected document. So could we please bear that in mind in our further proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Registrar, document P3314 is under seal. I wish everyone a good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
